2.3.4 Transportation of gases
We know that air is a mixture of gases, that fills the lungs and the
alveoli when enters our body.
The relative amount of different gases in air
and their combining capacity with haemoglobin and other substances in
blood determine their transport via blood in the body.
When oxygen present in the air is within normal limits (around 21%)
then almost all of it is carried in the blood by binding to haemoglobin
which is present in the red blood cells.
Haemoglobin is also a coloured
pigment like chlorophyll the only major difference being it has Iron (Fe+)
molecule in place of Magnesium (Mg+) as in chlorophyll.
As oxygen is diffused in the blood, it rapidly combines with the
haemoglobin to form oxyhaemoglobin.
Not only haemoglobin can combine
with oxygen, but the reverse can also happen to yield a molecule of
haemoglobin and oxygen at the tissue level.
Carbon dioxide is usually transported as bicarbonate, while some
amount of it combines with haemoglobin and rest is dissolved in blood
plasma.
Study the following equation for better understanding.
Hb + 4O2 Hb(O2)4 (in lungs)
Hb(O2)4 Hb + 4O2 (in tissues)

2.8 Evolution in gases exchanging system
Exchange of gases is a common life process in all living organisms,
but it is not same in all.
Single celled organisms Amoeba or multicellular
organisms like Hydra, Planaria, roundworms and earthworms obtain
oxygen and expel carbon dioxide directly from the body by the process of
diffusion.
In other multicellular animals special organs are evolved.
Animals
either terrestrial or aquatic adapted to different types of respiration and
possess different types of respiratory organs mostly depending on the
habitat in which they live.
Body size, availability of water and the type of
their circulatory system are some of the factors for the animals to develop
different types of respiratory organs.
There is tracheal respiratory system in insects like cockroach,
grasshopper etc.
Tracheal respiratory system consists of series of tubes
called trachea.
This is divided into fine branches called tracheoles which
carry air directly to the cells in the tissues.
Some aquatic animals like fishes have developed special organs for
respiration which are known as gills or branchiae.
Blood supplied to gills
through capillaries which have thin walls where gases are exchanged.
This
is called branchial respiration (gill respiration).
Fish keeps its mouth open
and lowers the floor of the oral cavity.
As a result water from outside will
be drawn into the oral cavity.
Now the mouth is closed and the floor of the
oral cavity is raised.
Water is pushed into the pharynx and is forced to gill
pouches through internal branchial apertures.
Gill lamellae are bathed with
water and absorbs the oxygen dissolved in the water.

2.9 Respiration in Plants
You already know about stomata in leaf where
gaseous exchange takes place in plants.
There are
other areas on the plant body as well through which
gaseous exchange take place like surface of aerial
roots, lenticels on stem etc.
Some plants have
specialized structures like breathing roots of
mangrove plants that produces oxygen is also
required by plants to produce energy and carbon
dioxide is released.
2.9.1 Transportation of gases in plants
The stomatal openings lead to a series of spaces
between the cells inside the plant.
Which form a
continuous network all over the plant.
The spaces
are very large in the leaves, much smaller in other
parts of the plant.
The air spaces are lined with water
where the oxygen is dissolved in this and passes
through the porous cell walls into the cytoplasm.
Here the glucose is broken down into carbon dioxide
and water with the liberation of the energy.
The
energy released is stored in mitochondria in the form
of A TP to perform metabolic activities.
The carbon dioxide passes out into the air spaces
by a similar method.
The whole system works by
diffusion as the oxygen is used up by the cells a
gradient develops between the cells and the air in
the spaces.

parsed_output.answer: Alveoli are designed to maximize the exchange of gases due to their structural features. They are numerous, which increases the surface area for gas exchange. Each alveolus is surrounded by a network of blood capillaries, allowing for efficient diffusion of oxygen into the blood and carbon dioxide out of the blood. Additionally, the walls of the alveoli and capillaries are only one cell thick, which further facilitates the exchange of gases by reducing the distance they need to travel.

required_point_details.point: Alveoli are extremely numerous microscopic air sacs
Their folding/number gives an enormous moist surface area
They are closely associated with blood capillaries
These features support rapid gas exchange by diffusion
